title: Assessing the technical rating of a lift
summary: NH introduces a lift's technical rating: how much practice it takes to master a lift and keep that mastery. High-rated lifts like the Olympic lifts, full front squats and ring skills cost time and tonnage. Isolation and bodyweight moves sit low. Bodybuilders should keep compounds frequent and avoid or simplify elite technical lifts.
claims: A lift's technical rating is how much practice it takes to master it and keep mastery high
Bodybuilders want mastery kept high so strength gains reflect muscle gains, not neural learning
Neural adaptation happens in a learning phase, not over years; once proficient, strength gains come from muscle unless you change form
People who constantly rotate lifts keep relearning them and aren't really progressing
Keep movement patterns frequent, several times a week, via variations and rotations
Include very technical lifts only sparingly; you can't maintain 15 of them
Olympic weightlifters train snatch and clean and jerk at very high frequency because their technical ceiling is so high
Curls, lateral raises and wrist curls have low technical ratings: quick to master and retained without practice
Multi-joint lifts like bench, squat and deadlift are harder to retain; squatting once a month means relearning it each time
Bench strength drops fast at low frequency because it's hard to progress and easy to regress; deadlifts tolerate low frequency because many muscles make them easy to load
Stop overhead pressing for a month and you'll lose a lot of strength
High-rated compounds should appear mostly in conventional form, with more variations and frequency, since they drive tonnage; isolation can be trained less often
Bodyweight moves like pull-ups and push-ups have low technical rating but should be done often because they're easy to recover from
Bodybuilders shouldn't do full snatches or clean and jerks; use block or partial variations that lower the technical rating
You must reach mastery before progressive overload targets muscle rather than learning, which costs time and tonnage
Olympic lifters don't curl and powerlifters stick to the big three because maintaining mastery leaves no time
He would tell his past self not to learn the front squat: it took years to master and he loses thoracic extension within a week without practice
He now must front squat plus a front squat variation weekly, sometimes twice, a prisoner of his own investment
No technical lift is necessary; the middle ground suffices unless a lift really inspires you
Front squats with crossed arms or an SSB have a lower technical rating than a proper clean-grip front rack
Elite ring skills cost leg size and tonnage; easy ring variations still give good hypertrophy
Lower a lift's technical rating with easier variations; once you invest in a skill you must maintain it or lose the investment
Wasted time is wasted tonnage, and wasted tonnage is lost muscle
exercises: clean-grip front rack; needs thoracic extension
high technical rating, he regrets the investment
